chunks.text: Right, we're recording. Can you see the code on my screen? Yeah. It's a bit small but I can zoom in. Great. Today is algorithms and programming techniques. This one is intentionally more practice-heavy. Before we start, how did your basketball game go? We lost by two points. Ah unlucky. Okay, coding now. Let's begin with linear search. Suppose we have the list 14, 7, 23, 5, 19 and we want to find 5. We check from the first item until we find five. Exactly. Linear search checks items one by one. It does not require the data to be sorted. Worst case, if the target is at the end or missing, we may inspect every element. So it's simple but can be slow. Correct. Now write pseudocode. set index to zero, found false, while index is less than length and found is false... if array index equals target then found true, otherwise index plus one. Good. Notice the loop condition prevents us going beyond the end. Before we move on, what if the target appears twice? This version stops at the first one. Exactly. We are still discussing linear search; 'before we move on' here is not a topic change. Let's test it. target nineteen. index zero fourteen no, index one seven no, index two twenty-three no, index three five no, index four nineteen yes. found true. Great.

Let's move on to binary search. This is a new algorithm. Binary search requires the list to be sorted. We repeatedly compare the target with the middle item and discard half of the remaining search area. So if the target is smaller than the middle, we only keep the left half. Correct. If greater, keep the right half. Example: 3, 8, 12, 17, 25, 31, 42. Search for 31. Middle is 17, 31 is bigger, so right side. Then middle of the remaining section is around 31, and we find it quickly. Binary search is generally more efficient on large sorted datasets because each comparison removes about half the remaining items. But remember the requirement: sorted data. sorted data. That's the catch. Could we sort first and then binary search? Sometimes, but sorting itself has a cost. The right choice depends on the situation.... if you're only searching one tiny list, linear search may be perfectly reasonable. Okay next question. Compare linear and binary search in words. Linear checks each item and works on unsorted data. Binary keeps halving the search area but needs sorted data. Excellent. Now, let's move on to sorting algorithms. Start with bubble sort. Bubble sort compares adjacent items and swaps them if they are in the wrong order. After a full pass, a large value can 'bubble' toward the end. Example: 5, 2, 4, 1. Compare 5 and 2, swap: 2, 5, 4, 1. Compare 5 and 4, swap: 2, 4, 5, 1. Compare 5 and 1, swap: 2, 4, 1, 5. Then we do another pass. Right. Compare 2 and 4 no swap. Compare 4 and 1 swap, giving 2, 1, 4, 5. Then another pass gives 1, 2, 4, 5. We may optimise by stopping if a full pass makes no swaps. So a flag variable? Exactly, maybe swapped equals false at the start of each pass. This is a good place to connect algorithms to programming constructs: loops, variables, Boolean flags, array indexing. wait, did I say compare 2 and 4 twice? I did. Ignore the repeated sentence, the final order is correct. Let's move on to merge sort. Merge sort uses divide and conquer. Split the list into smaller lists until each contains one item, then merge them back in sorted order. Take 8, 3, 6, 2. Split into 8,3 and 6,2. Then into single elements. Merge 8 and 3 as 3,8. Merge 6 and 2 as 2,6. Finally merge 3,8 with 2,6 to get 2,3,6,8. It's more complicated than bubble sort. Conceptually, yes. But it can be much more efficient for large datasets. For GCSE, be able to describe how the algorithm works and trace examples. Okay, before we move on, let's compare bubble and merge sort. Bubble sort repeatedly compares adjacent values. Merge sort splits and merges. And both result in sorted data. Correct. We're still in sorting here, not a new topic.

Now let's move on to trace tables and dry running code. A trace table records how variables change as an algorithm executes. Suppose total equals zero. For i from zero to three, total equals total plus array i. Array is 2, 4, 1, 3. So total is 2, then 6, then 7, then 10. Yes. A trace table might have columns for i and total. Now here's a common bug: using i less than or equal to array length. Why is that wrong? Because last valid index is length minus one. Exactly. For length four, indices are zero, one, two, three. Index four is outside the array. This is an off-by-one error. Let's do a longer dry run because I want you to practise keeping context over many lines. count equals zero, max equals array zero, then for i from one while i is less than array length. If array i is greater than max, set max to array i and increment count. Array values are 4, 9, 2, 11, 11, 5, 18, 7, 21, 3. At i one, 9 greater than 4, max becomes 9 and count one. Good. i two, 2 not greater. i three, 11 greater, max eleven and count two. i four is also eleven so not greater. Correct because condition is greater than, not greater than or equal. i five 5 no. i six 18 yes, max eighteen count three. i seven 7 no. i eight 21 yes, max twenty-one count four. i nine 3 no. So the final max is twenty-one and count is four. Count tells us how many times a new maximum was found. Exactly. Let's think about it again, again. If the condition had greater than or equal, the second eleven would also increment count. That's a subtle detail exam questions like. Okay, I know this is long, but we are intentionally staying on the same trace-table problem for a while. Now change the array to 10, 8, 6, 4, 2. What happens? Max starts ten, nothing is greater, so count stays zero. Exactly. sorry. Next, let's talk about subroutines and parameters. A procedure performs a task; a function returns a value. Depending on the language and specification wording, terminology can vary, so focus on the course definitions. Parameters are values passed into a subroutine. Arguments are the actual values used when calling it. Like function add a comma b, then add 3 comma 4? Yes. a and b are parameters; 3 and 4 are arguments in that call. Local variables exist within the subroutine's scope. Why use subroutines? Decomposition, reuse, easier testing, easier maintenance, clearer structure. So instead of copying the same code. Exactly.

Now let's move on to validation and authentication—careful, they sound similar but they're not. Validation checks whether input is sensible or follows rules. It does not prove the data is true. Range check, length check, type check, presence check, format check. Verification is checking it was entered correctly? Right. Double entry or visual checks are examples of verification methods. Authentication is different again: checking identity, for example username and password or two-factor authentication. I'm mentioning authentication because students often confuse the words, but don't merge it with validation in your notes. Okay. Last coding point: Boolean logic in conditions. AND requires both conditions true. OR requires at least one true. NOT reverses a Boolean value. If age is greater than or equal to 13 AND consent is true, then access allowed. Both parts matter. With OR, either one can be true. Correct. Let's finish. What were the big areas today? linear search, binary search, bubble and merge sort, trace tables, subroutines, validation, and Boolean logic. Good. Authentication was mentioned as a contrast as well. Sorry I have another call now, so we'll stop there. okay bye. bye.
